questions.q: What is Jimmy Carter's central claim about faith in lesson 1?
a: It reaches far beyond religion into nearly every part of life
It only matters to people who belong to an organized church
It should be based on a fixed set of unexamined dogmas
It is a private feeling that has little effect on society
questions.why: Lesson 1 argues that almost everyone trusts in something, religious or not.

questions.q: How does Carter suggest a believer should treat moments of doubt?
a: As a natural opening to search harder and deepen belief
As a warning sign that faith was never genuine
As something to hide from one's religious community
As a problem solved by avoiding difficult questions
questions.why: Lesson 2 frames doubt as part of a sincere search rather than a threat.

questions.q: What did Carter do after his father died at 59?
a: He looked for answers more eagerly than he had before
He stopped attending church for several years
He abandoned his study of theology altogether
He wrote a book arguing that God does not exist
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the loss pushed him to search for answers instead of erasing his faith.

questions.q: According to Carter, how do science and religion relate?
a: They complement each other by covering different parts of experience
They are rival explanations and one must eventually win
They are both useful only in their earliest forms
They should be kept completely separate in public life
questions.why: Lesson 3 says each describes a different area of the human experience.

questions.q: Rather than a fixed set of dogmas, what does Carter say religion should be?
a: A constant search for higher truth
A weekly routine of ritual and attendance
A set of rules passed down by a supreme authority
A personal code built without any community
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes religious belief as an ongoing pursuit of higher truth.
